name: deep gluteal syndrome
aliases: deep gluteal space sciatic nerve entrapment

reference.source: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Describes non-discogenic entrapment of the sciatic nerve within the deep gluteal (subgluteal) space, presenting as posterior hip and buttock pain with sciatica not attributable to the lumbar spine.
Symptoms are characteristically aggravated by prolonged sitting, and patients often shift weight or cannot tolerate sitting for extended periods.

Piriformis syndrome is one subset; entrapment may equally arise from fibrovascular bands, the obturator internus and gemelli, proximal hamstring pathology, ischiofemoral narrowing or vascular structures.
Provocation tests include the seated piriformis stretch test, the active piriformis test, and the flexion-adduction-internal-rotation manoeuvre; the Pace and Freiberg signs may also be positive.
A normal lumbar spine examination and imaging in a patient with sciatica should prompt consideration of an extraspinal source in the deep gluteal space.
MR neurography helps localise the entrapment site and characterise the nerve, while lumbar imaging is needed to exclude a discogenic cause.
Management begins with physiotherapy emphasising neural mobilisation and stretching, alongside image-guided perineural injection that is both therapeutic and diagnostic.
Endoscopic sciatic nerve decompression offers good outcomes in correctly selected patients who fail conservative treatment.
reference.pathophysiology: The deep gluteal or subgluteal space is bounded anteriorly by the posterior hip capsule and proximal femur, posteriorly by gluteus maximus, medially by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments and the ischium, and superiorly by the sciatic notch. The sciatic nerve courses through this space and may be compressed or tethered by several structures: the piriformis, including anatomical variants in which the nerve or its divisions pierce or straddle the muscle; fibrovascular bands; hypertrophied or inflamed short external rotators such as the obturator internus and gemelli; proximal hamstring scarring; a narrowed ischiofemoral interval; or aberrant vessels. Loss of the normal gliding and excursion of the nerve, often dynamic and posture-dependent, produces neuropathic buttock and posterior thigh pain.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar radiculopathy from disc herniation or stenosis
Intra-articular hip pathology such as a labral tear
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the pelvis and hip with MR neurography of the sciatic nerve
MRI of the lumbar spine to exclude a discogenic cause
Electrodiagnostic studies including nerve conduction studies and EMG, with positional testing where available
Dynamic ultrasound of the sciatic nerve in the deep gluteal space
Image-guided perineural diagnostic local anaesthetic injection
redFlags: Progressive motor weakness or foot drop indicating significant nerve compromise
Bowel or bladder dysfunction or saddle anaesthesia, suggesting cauda equina syndrome from a central cause
Constant severe night pain with systemic features, raising concern for a pelvic or presacral mass
Bilateral symptoms with rapidly evolving neurological signs
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with conservative treatment and image-guided perineural injection. Endoscopic decompression provides good pain relief and functional recovery in appropriately selected patients with a clearly identified entrapment, although recovery of longstanding neurological deficit can be incomplete.
pitfalls: Anchoring on a diagnosis of piriformis syndrome and overlooking the other entrapment sites within the deep gluteal space.
Failing to exclude the lumbar spine as the true pain generator before attributing symptoms to the deep gluteal space.
Relying on normal static imaging, since entrapment is frequently dynamic and posture-dependent.
Injecting near the sciatic nerve without image guidance, risking intraneural injection and nerve injury.
references: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
management: Begin with conservative treatment: activity modification avoiding prolonged sitting, and physiotherapy with sciatic nerve gliding and stretching of the piriformis and short external rotators
Provide analgesia with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and neuropathic agents for the neuropathic pain component
Offer image-guided perineural injection, with local anaesthetic and corticosteroid or botulinum toxin to the piriformis, for both diagnosis and treatment
Confirm the entrapment site with MR neurography and exclude a discogenic cause with lumbar spine imaging before invasive treatment
Refer for endoscopic sciatic nerve decompression in selected patients with a clearly identified entrapment refractory to conservative care
Counsel that recovery of a longstanding neurological deficit may be incomplete
